name: Ian Huang (shaoruu.io)
tagline: Personal site rendered as a walkable 3D voxel world
description: The personal site of Shaoru Ian Huang, an engineer at Cursor, built as an in-browser voxel world using his own Voxelize engine instead of a normal page layout. Around the canvas sit four plain sections — Cursor Resources, Lab, Milestones and Gallery — listing projects (Voxelize, TypeHere, Lunar Lander), career milestones (including a Microsoft DMCA strike) and generative art. A live visitor counter sits in the hero. It is a reference point for developer portfolios that treat the site itself as the demo.
agent_guidance: Treat this as visual inspiration only — the interesting half is a WebGL voxel canvas that you cannot read, so do not try to scrape layout or component patterns from the DOM. Reach for it when a user wants a portfolio whose hero IS the project (engine, game, tool) rather than a screenshot of it, and pair it with a real 3D stack (three.js / react-three-fiber) since Voxelize is a full server-backed voxel engine, not a drop-in widget. The surrounding text sections are conventional and safe to imitate.
why_it_matters: A clear example of the 'the site is the demo' portfolio, where the medium proves the engineering claim better than a case study would. Useful as a counterweight to the template-identical developer portfolio.
evidence: https://shaoruu.io/ (WebFetch + raw HTML fetch; text sections server-rendered, 3D scene is canvas-only). depo.zip's 'multiplayer personal website' claim could NOT be verified — no websocket, room, presence or player references appear in the served HTML, so multiplayer is not asserted here.

name: React Joyride
tagline: Guided product tours for React, v3 with a hook API
description: React Joyride turns an array of step definitions into an overlaid, step-by-step product tour with beacons, tooltips and a dimmed backdrop. Version 3 adds a useJoyride hook returning { controls, on, Tour } alongside the classic <Joyride steps run /> component, is roughly 30% smaller than v2, supports React 16.8 through 19, and server-renders under Next.js and Remix. Docs cover Props, Options, Styles, Floating Options, Step, Events, Custom Components, Recipes, Accessibility and a v2 migration guide. It is the default choice for onboarding walkthroughs in a React app.
agent_guidance: Default to this over hand-rolling a tour or over react-spotlight-tour: it is the only React tour library with real momentum (7.8k stars, v3.2.0 shipped July 2026) and it already handles focus trapping, keyboard nav and SSR. Install the matching agent skill with `npx skills add gilbarbara/react-joyride` before writing steps — the v2→v3 API changed and stale training data will hand you the old callback prop instead of the new `onEvent` / `useJoyride` shape. Watch out that steps target selectors that exist at run time; a missing target silently stalls the tour, so gate `run` on the mount of the target screen.
why_it_matters: The de facto standard for React product tours, and one of the few onboarding libraries that treats focus management and SSR as first-class rather than afterthoughts.
evidence: https://react-joyride.com/, https://react-joyride.com/docs, https://github.com/gilbarbara/react-joyride, npm registry API for react-joyride (latest 3.2.0, published 2026-07-09, MIT), GitHub API for gilbarbara/react-joyride (7835 stars, pushed 2026-07-09).

name: React Spotlight Tour
tagline: Tiny ref-based React tour overlay, unmaintained since 2021
description: A small React tutorial library from Revere CRE: you attach the ref returned by useSpotlight('some text') to any element, wrap the tree in <SpotlightTour>, and it dims the page and spotlights each element in turn. It needs no CSS import and the Spotlight renderer can be lazy-loaded, so the added bundle weight is small. The docs site is a real Docusaurus build with usage examples and a live demo, but the package has not been published since v1.1.0 in June 2021 and the repo sits at 19 stars.
agent_guidance: Do not reach for this by default — the last npm publish was v1.1.0 in June 2021, it has 19 stars, and it makes no accessibility claims, so use React Joyride for any product tour that ships. It is worth reading only when you need the opposite tradeoff: a ~zero-config, no-CSS, ref-per-element API where the tour order comes from render order rather than a steps array. If you do adopt it, pin the version, verify it against your React 19 tree yourself, and expect to add focus management by hand.
why_it_matters: A neat demonstration of the self-configuring, ref-driven tour API, but it has been dormant for years and should be read as a design reference rather than a dependency.
evidence: https://reverecre.github.io/react-spotlight-tour/, https://github.com/reverecre/react-spotlight-tour, npm registry API for react-spotlight-tour (latest 1.1.0, published 2021-06-09, MIT), GitHub API (19 stars, pushed 2026-02-13, not archived). npmjs.com page itself returned 403 to WebFetch, so version data came from registry.npmjs.org.

name: Wallspace
tagline: Native Swift live wallpapers for macOS, free tier plus $12.99 Pro
description: Wallspace is a macOS-native (Swift, not Electron) live wallpaper app that plays 4K video wallpapers on the desktop and, on macOS 26+, the lock screen. It claims under 2% CPU, pauses playback on battery or under load, supports a different wallpaper per display, accepts any local MP4 as a wallpaper, and has an AI search that maps a described mood or scene onto the library. The free tier is usable without an account or ads; Pro is a one-time $12.99 that unlocks lock screen, premium collections, custom wallpapers and auto-rotation. Requires macOS 15.0 or later.
pricing_detail: Free tier $0 forever (curated wallpapers, no download limits, background playback). Pro $12.99 one-time (list $15.49) — lock screen wallpapers, premium collections, custom wallpapers, multi-monitor, auto-change, community uploads, priority support. Multi-Mac licences: 2 Macs $19.49, 3 Macs $27.28, 5 Macs $38.97. 5-day refund policy. Payments via Polar. Publisher: Tangent Labs LLP.
agent_guidance: This is a consumer desktop utility, not a design dependency — never suggest it as part of a build. Surface it only when a user wants a desk-setup or wallpaper answer for a Mac, and lead with the hard constraints: macOS 15.0 minimum, lock screen support needs macOS 26, and the free tier withholds lock screen and custom-MP4 wallpapers. The site 403s a plain WebFetch, so re-check any claim with a browser user agent before quoting stats.
why_it_matters: One of the few live wallpaper apps for macOS built natively in Swift with a one-time price instead of a subscription, which is why it keeps getting recommended over the App Store alternatives.
notable_for: lock screen live wallpapers on macOS 26+
evidence: https://wallspace.app/ and https://wallspace.app/pricing, both fetched with curl and a browser user agent — WebFetch got HTTP 403 on both. Stats quoted on the homepage (20k active users, 100k wallpapers downloaded, 1,000+ total wallpapers, 800+ Discord members) are the vendor's own numbers and were not independently checked.

name: Skills.sh
tagline: Cross-agent skill registry with a one-command installer
description: Skills.sh indexes agent skills published on GitHub and installs them into whichever coding agent you use with `npx skills add <owner/repo>`. The front page is a live install leaderboard (All Time / Trending 24h / Hot / Official) — over 1.2 million installs recorded, with 600 ranked skills in the page payload and topic browsing across React, Next.js, Design & UI, Mobile, Agent workflows, Databases, Testing and Marketing. It writes config for more than twenty agents including Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Gemini, Cline, OpenCode, Zed, Goose and Kiro CLI, and also ships Packs, per-agent pages, audits, a CLI doc and an API.
agent_guidance: Use this when the user asks for a skill by capability and you do not already know its repo — `npx skills add <owner/repo>` resolves and writes the config for the host agent, so prefer it over telling the user to clone a repo into .claude/skills by hand. It is stack-wide rather than design-specific: for UI and design-engineering work, cross-check ui-skills.com first, which curates the same underlying SKILL.md files with far more editorial filtering. Treat the leaderboard as popularity, not quality — install counts are dominated by a handful of vendor bundles (Feishu/Lark alone occupies a dozen of the top slots), and skill licences vary per repo, so read the SKILL.md before you run it.
why_it_matters: The closest thing the agent-skill ecosystem has to npm's front page, and the only installer that normalises one command across twenty-plus coding agents.
evidence: https://skills.sh (WebFetch plus raw HTML, from which 600 leaderboard entries and the agent list were parsed), https://skills.sh/docs/cli, https://skills.sh/skills. https://skills.sh/llms.txt returns the Next.js 404 shell and https://skills.sh/leaderboard is 404, so no machine index was confirmed beyond /docs/api; 600 is the count present in the page payload, not a stated catalogue total.

name: UI Skills
tagline: 209 curated design-engineering skills, with MCP and llms.txt
description: UI Skills is Julien Thibeaut's (ibelick) curated catalogue of 209 agent skills aimed specifically at interface quality — accessibility, motion, systems, visual, interaction, performance, craft and taste. Rather than making you pick, it ships a router: an agent runs `npx ui-skills start`, then categories / list / get, and loads only the smallest relevant SKILL.md. The catalogue aggregates work from Anthropic, Vercel Labs, shadcn, antfu, addyosmani, emilkowalski, AccessLint, MengTo and others, plus ibelick's own baseline-ui, improve-ui, create-design-md and fixing-* skills. Everything is exposed three ways: the CLI, a hosted MCP server at /mcp with list_skills and get_skill, and plain text at /llms.txt and /skills/registry.txt.
agent_guidance: Start every UI task here rather than at skills.sh: run `npx ui-skills start` and let ui-skills-root route by topic and stack, because loading one 3KB SKILL.md beats pulling a general design skill into context. If the host supports MCP, register https://www.ui-skills.com/mcp instead and call list_skills/get_skill — that skips the npx cold start and keeps the catalogue fresh. Do not hand-pick from the visible grid: the site explicitly tells agents not to, and the registry at /skills/registry.txt maps every entry to a raw GitHub SKILL.md you can diff or vendor if you need to pin a version.
why_it_matters: The best-curated entry point for design-engineering agent skills — it solves selection, not just discovery, which is the actual failure mode when an agent has 200 skills available.
notable_for: router skill instead of manual picking
evidence: https://www.ui-skills.com/ and https://www.ui-skills.com/skills and https://www.ui-skills.com/mcp/docs (all fetched with curl and a browser user agent — WebFetch got HTTP 403), https://www.ui-skills.com/llms.txt, https://www.ui-skills.com/skills/registry.txt (209 tab-separated rows), GitHub API for ibelick/ui-skills (7234 stars, MIT, pushed 2026-08-13), npm registry for ui-skills (0.2.4, 2026-07-20, MIT).
